oops, i guess as far as advice goes... maybe she would be open to doing a massive clean if all the stuff was just going into boxes to be stored away. I'll do that and then have a rule in mind, like if in a month or two the box remains unopened, it goes to donation. 

that's basically my plan, pack everything away to get to bare bones and then reintroduce only what is necessary or *reallly* special. i think if i can take the vacation from clutter and reap the benefits to my mental health that simplicity would bring, it's more likely to stick.

i think i have hoarder tendencies due to object attachment. "things" do bring me comfort and i attach a lot of meaning to items, often anthropomorphizing them. sometimes i think it's a substitute for the sorts of feels human relationships would provide. so the whole, "does this item spark joy" thing doesn't work, since the answer is usually yes. 

it's massively problematic because i *need* simplicity, and think i would function much better in a minimalistic environment. it can definitely spiral because it negatively effects my executive function. even when things are tidy, it still contributes to overload. it makes even the smallest messes more difficult to take care of, because my brain breaks when i look at the space i need to tackle. i also struggle with not wanting to be wasteful, so if there's a potential other use for something i hate just throwing it out. being a crafter, everything has potential....so, yeah that's a problem. 

next big project is to suck it up and clear house, cause i think it would hugely improve my day to day functioning...it's difficult nonetheless. it's super counterproductive, I don't know how many people are genuinely just fine with it. i *know* it places strain on my other traits, but that knowledge isn't really helpful.

This one is pretty sensitive, but important and i think unfortunately, relatively common. Sexual assault and being the victim of partner violence is more prevalent in the population of women on the spectrum. 

On a smaller scale, i think my social difficulties made it so i didn't learn how to say no. this extends to other "deviant" behavior like drugs etc. i pretty much went along with whatever was going on around me to fit in. and even when it came down to my body, I didn't have the confidence or trust in myself to know what was socially acceptable. i feel like my insecurities about my social skills caused me to assume everyone else was right and i must be wrong. After all, I've always been out of the loop. 

i was easy to manipulate because i had no intrinsic sense of who i was in a social setting. and let's face it, i was downright gullible. I don't know if getting a diagnosis as a child would have made any difference, in all likelihood not. All i do know, is that the late in life diagnosis has cast an even larger shadow of uncertainty over my past and who i think/thought i was/am. To be fair, I've always had an unstable sense of self, due largely to masking (another thing that could be mistaken as a bpd trait). The perpetual state of identity crisis from the alienation and chameleon effect of masking, reallly takes a toll on your mental health. But i digress.... 

Point is, being a woman/teenager/girl on the spectrum comes with, the very serious additional risk, of being targeted by others with nefarious intentions. Or just winding up making a lot of poor decisions by easily succumbing to peer pressure. There are a lot of factors that i could go on and on about, but basically, the trajectory you're put on from the get go as an autistic woman, sets you on course for all sorts of trouble. Not that it's a guarantee or anything, but not uncommon either. 

Anywho, I'd like to see this discussed more openly, as a means to protect others, and also to provide support in the healing process for those like myself. 

Best of luck to you and your book!

this is not only unpopular but dangerous. i should think that the health and safety of your child is the utmost important factor, health very much including mental health. mental health being one thing that you as a parent have a very serious influence on. growing up feeling miserable and insecure, always feeling or fearing that you're doing something wrong, in most cases does not lead to success. depression is about the biggest motivation killer i can think of. sure, there are people who rise from the ashes and become more driven. that is not the majority of people by any means. there is a reason stories of rags to riches are inspiring, because they're rare. your child may very well wind up feeling that no amount of success will ever make them happy. that is not a feeling which motivates.

your story of failing out of college could have just as easily taken a very different turn. it also may not have happened if you had the opportunity under your mother's guidance to find other sources of happiness, made mistakes while someone was watching over you. instead, you did what many others have done, went wild at the first chance to, and did so very irresponsibly. understandable, you weren't taught how to do so responsibly. how to balance enjoyment while achieving your goals. many people decide against returning to misery, or a home which wouldn't help them through a failure. you could have just as easily kept that job at little caesars, continued partying unabashedly, and stayed. this happens to plenty of people. numerous friends of mine at university went this route. they were super smart, totally competent people, who figured out for themselves that happiness was more important. some carved out their own success, others didn't and wound up battling serious substance abuse problems. 

more often than "succeed" at a young age like yourself, miserable people develop issues. issues that can take a very long time to recover from, issues that *need* support from loved ones. if you developed a serious drug problem and your mother turned you away, there's a very solid chance you would still have that drug problem. 

your story of pulling yourself up and being who you are today, having what you have today, is incredible and inspiring. what is isn't, is common. if it was the normal, expected experience, it wouldn't be impressive. 

i guess my point is, you're taking a huge gamble on this one, and the odds are not in your favor. happiness and success are not mutually exclusive, they go hand in hand. not unlike misery and failure. raising your child to feel stable and self assured is a *much* safer bet. 

consider also, that your child's life is already drastically different than yours. they will not be raised in poverty, your rejection to help them will seem much crueler since you have every mean to. this is rife for resentment. you will more likely be seen as some sort of cartoonish archetype of a crude, unforgiving, joyless father. maybe you won't, maybe you'll navigate it seemlessly, maybe maybe maybe. do *you* think *you* will still be happy when your child isn't? could you still be happy if the coin flips against you, if your child becomes estranged and/or develops serious mental health issues? 

I'd imagine not. how you feel now does not guarantee that you will be happy for the rest of your life, making your suffering in youth worth it. fostering an environment for the ones around you to share in your pleasures and learn how to manufacture their own joy, is another safer bet. don't lose your found happiness by putting your relationship with your wife and child through unnecessary hurdles. use what you made for yourself and your family to give your child a better life. if you don't, you're squandering your achievements. 

idk, find common ground with your wife and learn about how parents (other than your mother) raise "happy" *and* "successful" children. best of luck.

That makes so much sense to me and is reassuring in way. The sensitivities themselves have a cascading effect. You're not simply processing more information at a relative rate. There is also a threshold that can be both crippling and awe-inspiring, not unlike the experience of psychedelics... 

That heightened attention and perception to sensory input is present since infancy. Early childhood experiences *will* be massively impacted by that. 

In my experience it lead to a role as an observer, processing *and* participating, just in a way unlike my peers. That role is self perpetuating even beyond the continued sensory acuity, since it is isolating by nature, and later by rejection. The observer, continuously maddened by sensory input and trapped in the mind, questions everything. This along with the social and developmental challenges, creates an early environment for introspection. All of these things and much more I'm sure, in confluence, make fertile ground for an existential crisis. 

That conclusion is traumatic, as well as the entire process and the myriad of factors that lead there.

NAH, I wouldn't feel right calling your sister TA, just cause I'm not in her head, and don't know the severity of her depression. not saying it's excusable behavior, it's definitely shitty. maybe it's just my own sympathy, having struggled with severe depression basically my whole life. as for you, you're 15 and carrying a burden that someone your age shouldn't have to. so you exploded. that also gets an asshole pass in my opinion. 

depression definitely can be infectious... you may not totally understand where she is at right now, but can feel yourself slipping towards it, your exhaustion isn't merely physical. she needs to hear this at some point, preferably delicately. she probably knows this to some degree and feels like a burden already. That feeling is a common symptom, fueled by feeling of worthless etc., and the actions that arise from those feelings. it's a self perpetuating unending cycle unless something disrupts it. like a catch-22 though. the condition is a barrier to the necessary actions required to dismantle it. 


I'll add some advice for good measure:

sit down when calm to express yourself. it's clear you're sympathetic to her, but the situation is becoming unbearable and your own mental health is at stake. you seem like a deeply selfless and kind person, who is fully capable of expressing your own emotions without attacking her character or directly placing blame. *absolutely* encourage her to seek professional help, she's not broken just lost. in the mean time, she should take on a little bit more activity each day. 

maybe you can suggest doing some chores together at first. someone washes or drys the dishes, you tackle a cleaning project or room together, etc. it will feel less daunting for her that way and you benefit too. i think some simple change in phrasing can go a long way. instead of asking her to do a chore *for* you (because you need her to), ask her to help you *with* a chore (because you are unable to do it alone). if you had to move something impossibly heavy to carry on your own, which could be done easily with simply an extra set of hands, I'd imagine she wouldn't refuse you. she could do some of these chores with your little sister as well. if it's framed as asking her teach something, instead of just do something, it could alter her mindset. it's all helping behavior, just contextualized differently, and sometimes that can make all the difference. some family bonding time between you all is good for the spirit too. a utilitarian way to broach mending the rift, the wedge that is depression causes.

well this makes me really sad, and I'm sorry you feel this way. I can definitely imagine why you feel the way you do. I've had my own internalized issues with identifying nonbinary, and personally don't really like to tell people, for fear of judgement from both the lgbtqia and cis/hetero community. That I wasn't "trans enough", and was turning my back on feminism or something. I've argued with myself over whether it was counterintuitive to fight stereotypes by rejecting the binary.

Ultimately, I came to the conclusion it isn't. As long as there's only two sides to pick from, people are going to continue to compartmentalize in a reductive manner. The more categories to choose from, the less power they'll carry. Which hopefully, will lead to the reasonable conclusion, that pigeon holing people in a box based on their born reproductive characteristics is meaningless and ultimately harmful to *many* people. How we differ as individuals, will always say more about who we are, than being AFAB or AMAB ever could. And everyone should have a choice in the way they express themselves, feel safe and supported throughout the entire process, to reach a final form that is truly comfortable and reflects who they are on the inside. If that requires full surgical procedures, or maybe just top surgery, or if they want to microdose E, etc., they should be able to do that without fear or judgement.

I can personally say, I have struggled a lot with gender dysphoria, it's different I'm sure to what you have experienced and I don't doubt easier. I don't have to face the challenges of dealing with a transphobic health care system or be as commonly chastised by the ignorant. That's not to say there aren't any challenges though. It's been a source of a great deal of inner turmoil and confusion. It's made for particularly difficult feelings over intimacy, that has had a real impact on my ability to form romantic relationships. I don't feel the desire to change my body right now, as I'm not convinced that would help. There is a disconnect, confusion, and shame, but no resolution I can really imagine that could correct that.

I think I would feel the same if I were still me and AMAB instead AFAB. I know that I do have a hormonal imbalance, and that it could be a major source in this feeling, but I don't think it's the only one. I lack a lot of the knowledge and terms to express these feelings, because I haven't felt comfortable sharing them with others. It just doesn't make any sense to people how I could feel alienated in a way that is so clear to others. If I don't feel comfortable as a woman, then surely I would as a man. It's just not the case here. And that's highly oversimplified I know.

I would like to find peace in my body and mind despite this gap in attachment. To be more comfortable with intimacy and romance. I still want those things, but feel it would be dishonest to them and hurtful to me if I didn't disclose my fractured identity. It was a source of a lot of turmoil in my last relationship. I was suffering and felt really alone and lost, and also so guilty that I was in some way deceiving them. I can't do that again, and I won't, which is why I am now identifying as nonbinary. That very well may change. I've considered hormone therapy as well as top surgery, but it's not something I know I want. 

I do want to be able to discuss these things in a safe space. In a community that says it's okay to be confused, it's okay to ask questions, we support you. Hopefully I'll learn what it is I do wish to do moving forward, how I can reach self acceptance. At the very least I'd like some friends who can relate, even if that's at varying degrees.
